title: Local SEO Basics: Google Business Profile, Citations, Reviews
excerpt: How Google picks local results, and how to set up your Business Profile, fix citations, earn reviews within the rules and build local pages that rank well.

content_html:
Say you run a dog grooming salon. Someone two streets away searches "dog groomer near me" on their phone. Google shows a map with a handful of businesses, and the person taps one of those three or four names. If yours is not there, you did not lose a ranking battle. You were never in the room. That is the problem local SEO solves.

That map-and-listings view is where local SEO lives. It is driven less by your website alone and more by your Google Business Profile, how consistently your business details appear across the web, and what customers say about you.

This guide covers the basics a small business can handle itself: how Google decides which local results to show, how to set up and optimize a Business Profile, citations and NAP consistency, reviews within Google's rules, local landing pages and LocalBusiness structured data.

Local listings and citations are one part of off-page SEO. Our guide to off-page SEO and authority covers the wider picture, including how links and mentions build trust.

How local SEO results are chosen

Google's help page on improving your local ranking says local results are mainly based on three things:

  • Relevance: how well a Business Profile matches what someone is searching for.
  • Distance: how far the business is from the person searching. If they do not share their location, Google uses what it knows about it.
  • Prominence: how well known the business is. Google says this is also based on information such as how many websites link to your business and how many reviews you have.

You cannot change your distance from a searcher, so local SEO is the work of improving relevance and prominence. Google also states there is no way to request or pay for a better local ranking.

That shapes your priorities. A complete, accurate profile improves relevance. Reviews, consistent citations and a well-known local reputation improve prominence.

Set up and optimize your Google Business Profile

Your Business Profile is the single most important local SEO asset. Claim it, verify it, and then make it complete.

Get the basics exactly right

  • Verify the profile. Google says verification makes the business more likely to show up in results.
  • Name: use your real-world business name, exactly as it appears on your signage and stationery.
  • Primary category: choose the most specific category that describes your core business ("Dog groomer", not just "Pet store"). Add secondary categories only if they are true.
  • Address or service area: use your real location. If you visit customers rather than having them visit you, set up a service area.
  • Hours: keep regular hours current and add special hours for holidays.
  • Phone and website: use a local number you answer, and link to the most relevant page of your site.

Avoid the shortcuts that get profiles suspended

Google's guidelines for representing your business are strict, and breaking them can lead to suspension. The most common mistakes:

  • Adding keywords or a location to the name. "Paws & Claws" is fine. "Paws & Claws Best Dog Grooming Springfield" is not, unless that is genuinely your registered, signposted name.
  • Using a virtual office or a mailbox address you do not operate from.
  • Creating more than one profile for the same location.
  • Choosing categories as keywords rather than to describe what you actually are.

Fill in the rest

Complete every relevant section: business description, services or products, attributes (such as wheelchair access or parking), and photos of your premises, team and work. Google's help pages note that businesses with complete and accurate information are more likely to show up for relevant searches.

Action: open your profile and fill in every empty field you can answer honestly. Then add at least five recent photos of real work.

NAP consistency and local citations

NAP stands for name, address and phone number. A citation is any mention of your business with those details: directories, industry listings, local chamber of commerce pages, review sites and social profiles.

Citations matter because they help Google and customers confirm that your business is real and where it is. The problem is inconsistency, which builds up over years as businesses move, change numbers or rebrand.

Where it appearsWhat it saysProblem
Business ProfilePaws & Claws, 12 High St, Unit 3Correct (the reference)
Old directory listingPaws and Claws Grooming, 40 Mill RdOld address from before a move
Website footerPaws & Claws, 12 High StreetMissing unit number
Social profileOld mobile numberWrong phone

Small formatting differences ("St" vs "Street") are usually harmless. Wrong addresses, old phone numbers and outdated names are what confuse customers and dilute trust.

A simple cleanup process:

  1. Decide on one canonical version of your name, address and phone, matching your Business Profile.
  2. Make sure your own website uses it exactly, in the footer and on the contact page.
  3. Search for your business name, old addresses and old phone numbers to find existing listings.
  4. Update or claim each listing, starting with the biggest directories and industry sites in your country and niche.
  5. Keep a spreadsheet of every listing and its login, so the next change takes minutes rather than days.

Earn and respond to reviews, within Google's rules

Reviews feed prominence directly, and they are often the deciding factor for the person comparing three businesses on a map.

Ask every happy customer, but never pay, bribe or filter. Google's policy on fake engagement prohibits businesses from:

  • Offering incentives (discounts, free services, payment) in exchange for reviews, or for changing or removing a negative review.
  • Discouraging or prohibiting negative reviews.
  • Selectively asking only happy customers for reviews (often called review gating).

What you can do is ask everyone, consistently. Google lets you create a review link or QR code from your profile. Put it on receipts, in follow-up emails and on a card at the counter.

Respond to reviews, too. Thank people specifically, and answer negative reviews calmly: acknowledge the issue, explain what you can do, and offer to continue the conversation privately. Future customers read your replies as much as the reviews themselves.

Build local landing pages that deserve to rank

Your website still matters for local SEO. Your Business Profile links to it, and it can rank in the regular results below the map.

  • One location: make your home page and contact page clearly local, with your full NAP, opening hours, an embedded map and the areas you serve.
  • Several locations: give each real location its own page, with its own address, hours, staff, photos and details.
  • Service areas: create area pages only where you genuinely serve customers and have something specific to say (local jobs, local regulations, travel times).

Avoid near-identical pages that swap in a town name. Google's spam policies treat pages created mainly to rank for slight variations of a search, like this, as doorway pages.

Each location page should also pass the basics in our on-page SEO checklist: a clear title, one H1, descriptive headings and useful content.

Add LocalBusiness structured data

LocalBusiness structured data describes your business in a machine-readable format: name, address, phone, hours and more. Google's LocalBusiness structured data documentation lists name and address as required, with properties like telephone, url, geo and openingHoursSpecification recommended.

A minimal example:

<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "LocalBusiness",
  "name": "Paws & Claws",
  "address": {
    "@type": "PostalAddress",
    "streetAddress": "12 High Street, Unit 3",
    "addressLocality": "Springfield",
    "postalCode": "12345",
    "addressCountry": "US"
  },
  "telephone": "+1-555-0100",
  "url": "https://example.com/"
}
</script>

Use the most specific subtype that fits, and keep the details identical to what is visible on the page and in your Business Profile. One common mistake: adding aggregateRating with your own reviews. Google recommends that property only for sites that capture reviews about other local businesses.

For a walkthrough of how JSON-LD works and how to test it, see our beginner's guide to structured data.

Show real people and real experience

Local customers want to know who will turn up at their door or greet them at the counter. Name your team, show photos of real jobs, and explain how long you have served the area. Our guide to showing experience and trust on every page covers these signals in more detail.

The bottom line

Local SEO comes down to three things you control: a complete and accurate Google Business Profile, consistent business details everywhere you are listed, and a steady flow of genuine reviews that you respond to. Distance is out of your hands, so relevance and prominence are where the work goes.

Your website backs it all up with clear local pages and structured data that matches what customers see. None of it is complicated, but it does need regular attention, because details go stale quietly.

Your next step: open your Google Business Profile today, correct anything that does not match your signage and website exactly, fill every empty field, and set up a review link to share with your next ten customers.

faqs.question: How long does local SEO take to work?
faqs.answer: Fixing errors in your Business Profile can make a difference fairly quickly once Google processes the change, but building prominence through reviews and citations takes months of steady effort. There is no fixed timeline, because it depends on your competition and how established your business already is.

faqs.question: Can I add keywords to my Google Business Profile name?
faqs.answer: No. Google's guidelines say your profile name must match your real-world business name as used on your signage and stationery. Adding keywords or locations that are not part of that name can lead to suspension.

faqs.question: Is it allowed to ask customers for Google reviews?
faqs.answer: Yes. Google allows businesses to ask customers to share genuine experiences. What is not allowed is offering incentives, discouraging negative reviews, or only asking customers you expect to be happy.

faqs.question: Do I need a website for local SEO?
faqs.answer: You can appear in local results with only a Business Profile, but a website helps. It gives your profile a page to link to, can rank in the regular results below the map, and lets you add LocalBusiness structured data and detailed location pages.
